title: Environmental and phylogenetic determinants of raptorial foreleg morphology in Zelus assassin bugs (Heteroptera: Reduviidae)
content:
Abstract
Understanding the relative roles of ecological adaptation and phylogenetic history in morphological diversification is a central question in evolutionary biology. Raptorial traits involved in prey capture are particularly informative because they directly affect performance and are expected to respond to environmental selection. This study investigated ecological and phylogenetic drivers of foreleg morphology in the assassin bug genus Zelus (Heteroptera: Reduviidae) using multilocus phylogenetic reconstruction and phylogenetically informed comparative analyses. Foreleg robustness was quantified using a thickness index (TI) based on femur dimensions and related to climatic, geographical, and habitat variables across 17 species distributed in the Americas. Phylogenetic analyses (maximum parsimony, maximum likelihood, and Bayesian inference) produced congruent topologies and strongly supported the monophyly of Zelus. However, TI showed weak phylogenetic signal, indicating limited evolutionary conservatism. Comparative models indicated that wetter and more forested environments are associated with higher TI, whereas elevation, climatic seasonality, and geographical range size are negatively associated with foreleg robustness. Ecological variables explained more variation in raptorial morphology than shared ancestry, suggesting that repeated ecological adaptation has been the main driver of trait evolution in Zelus. These results support the idea that performance-related traits can evolve rapidly in response to environmental gradients despite phylogenetic constraints.
